title: TBC launches Mischief 1 video API from $0.005 per second
dek: The Wan 2.2-based model reaches fal and OpenRouter with separate 480p and 720p prices and software derived from laboratory neuron research.
lede: The Biological Computing Co. launched Mischief 1 on fal and OpenRouter on October 30. Developers can turn images into short videos with a starting generation price of half a cent per second.

body.text: The model takes a first-frame image and a text prompt. A five-second generation costs $0.025 at 480p or $0.05 at 720p, based on OpenRouter’s listed rates. Resolution therefore doubles the generation bill for the same clip length.

TBC built Mischief 1 on Wan 2.2. The company says measurements of laboratory-grown neurons informed its software optimizations. Those neurons remain in the lab; customer inference runs on standard AI hardware. The release makes that software available through hosted video endpoints.

buildersNote: Budget $2.50 for 100 five-second clips at 480p, or $5 at 720p, before any other charges. Compare completed outputs on the same images before choosing a resolution.

claims.text: OpenRouter lists the October 30 release and both resolution-specific prices.
TBC says Mischief 1 is five times faster than Wan 2.2 while matching its quality.
The launch notice supplies no independent benchmark or reproducible method for that speed-and-quality comparison.

sources.title: The Biological Computing Co. Launches World’s First Publicly Available Neuron-Derived AI Video Model

social.voiceover: [matter-of-fact] Mischief One launched with image-to-video generation from half a cent per second. [break] Its software runs on ordinary AI hardware. The maker’s fivefold speed claim still lacks an independent benchmark.
social.short: Mischief 1 launched on fal and OpenRouter on October 30. Five seconds of 480p video costs $0.025. TBC’s fivefold speed claim lacks an independent benchmark in its announcement.
social.long:
TBC launched Mischief 1 on October 30, bringing its Wan 2.2-based video model to fal and OpenRouter. The software draws on lab neuron research and runs on standard AI hardware.

A five-second clip costs $0.025 at 480p or $0.05 at 720p. That sets a concrete budget for testing variations; the company’s fivefold speed claim still lacks an independent benchmark in its launch notice.
